title: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning
oneLiner: How a program can learn good behaviour by trying actions, collecting rewards and slowly working out which choices pay off in the long run.

what.html:
Reinforcement learning (RL) is learning by doing. An agent (the learner) looks at its situation, picks an action, and the world answers with a reward (a number saying how good that was) and a new situation. Nobody tells it the right move; it has to find out by trying, and it aims to collect as much reward as possible over time, not just right now.

Everyday versionTraining a dog with treats: you can't explain the rules, but you reward good behaviour, and the dog gradually works out which actions earn treats, including ones that only pay off after a sequence of steps.

why.html:
• Some problems have no "correct answer" to copy, only outcomes: games, robots, recommendations, controlling machines.
  • Often you can only learn by interacting, sometimes only in a simulator.
  • Good decisions now may only pay off much later, and RL is built for exactly that.

how.title: Learning from consequences
how.html: RL is an approach to a type of problem: making a sequence of decisions where the only feedback is a reward. Use it when the world is too complex to solve with a formula, when you only have a simulator, or when the only way to learn is to try things.

how.title: Not supervised, not unsupervised
how.html: Supervised learning copies labelled answers; unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabelled data. RL gets neither: it gets a score for what it did, and its own actions decide what data it sees next.

how.title: Why it's hard
how.html: There's no teacher, decisions come one after another, order matters, and rewards can arrive late. If you lose a game at move 40, which earlier move was the mistake? That puzzle is called credit assignment. The agent also has to balance exploring new moves against exploiting moves it already knows are good.

how.title: The loop
how.html: Observe the state → choose an action → receive a reward and the next state → repeat. The reward for the action at step t is labelled t + 1 because it comes back with the next state.

how.title: Four ingredients
how.html: Policy: how the agent picks actions (its habits). Reward: the immediate score. Value: how good a situation is in the long run (judgement). Model (optional): the agent's guess of what will happen next (imagination), used to plan ahead.

how.title: Nudging estimates
how.html: After each move, the agent moves its estimate for the previous position a little toward its estimate for the new position: new = old + α × (target − old). A small α learns slowly but steadily; a larger α reacts fast but jitters.

demo.html: This player keeps a table of "chance of winning" for every board it has seen. Press Train a few times and watch it learn against a random opponent. Try ε = 0 (never explore) or a very large α and compare.

example.html:
One update in tic-tac-toe. The current board is unknown, so its value is 0.5. X's greedy move creates three in a row, a board worth 1. With α = 0.1 the old board's value becomes 0.5 + 0.1 × (1 − 0.5) = 0.55. After thousands of games these small nudges turn the table into a good map of which positions win.

Supplementary Exploratory (random) moves aren't used to update values: they'd teach the value of playing randomly, not of playing well.

misunderstandings: RL is an approach; a simple lookup table can do it.
The reward tells the agent the right action.
It only scores the action that was taken.
Maximise long-run reward; values capture that.
Model-free methods learn straight from experience.
takeaways: RL learns from rewards earned by interacting, not from labelled answers.
It's sequential and feedback is delayed, which causes the credit-assignment problem.
The loop: state → action → reward and next state.
Policy, reward, value function and an optional model are the four elements.
Estimates are updated with new = old + α(target − old).
thirty: Reinforcement learning is an approach to sequential decision problems in which an agent learns by trial and error to maximise long-run reward. Unlike supervised learning (labelled answers) and unsupervised learning (structure in unlabelled data), RL receives only evaluative, often delayed, feedback, and its own actions generate its data, which creates the credit-assignment and exploration–exploitation problems. At each step the agent observes Sₜ, takes Aₜ and receives Rₜ₊₁ and Sₜ₊₁. An RL system has a policy, a reward signal, a value function and optionally a model. In tic-tac-toe, a table of win probabilities updated by V(s) ← V(s) + α[V(s′) − V(s)] learns to beat an imperfect opponent; the step size α trades convergence against tracking change.

check.q: What feedback does an RL agent receive?
opts: A reward for the action it took
